results.title: Gerry Gee
results.brief_description:
Ron Blaskett helped bring ventriloquism from the stage to Victoria’s first television screens. Born in Melbourne in 1922, Blaskett became one of Australia’s best-known ventriloquists, adapting live puppetry for a new broadcast audience.

Blaskett and Gerry Gee made television history together on 11 October 1956, introducing GTV-9’s test program. Gerry’s name was inspired by ‘GTV’, and the pair later appeared on Channel 9’s opening night in January 1957. At a time when television was still finding its language, their partnership helped fill the screen with live character, humour and personality.

Made for Blaskett by Chicago puppet maker Frank Marshall, Gerry Gee could roll his eyes upwards and poke out his tongue. He became a favourite on The Tarax Show, inspiring merchandise including Gerry Gee Junior dolls. Blaskett and Gerry performed together for almost 60 years.

results.title: The Ferals
results.brief_description:
The Ferals (1994–95) brought grunge energy and dark humour to Australian children’s television. Full of slang, 90s pop culture and backyard chaos, it followed four feral animals squatting in a shed: Rattus the rat, Modigliana the cat, Mixy the rabbit and Derryn the dog.

Designer Gareth Frost and puppet maker Tina Matthews drew on punk aesthetics to create hand and rod puppets that were lightweight but sturdy enough for cartoon violence. 

Puppeteers gave each character distinct personalities, blending unruly human and animal traits. Modigliana, or “Moddie”, was a stroppy diva often compared to Miss Piggy. Mixy’s erratic comedy carried a darker joke: myxomatosis, introduced to Australia to cull feral rabbits. The Ferals made children’s puppetry scruffy and unmistakably Australian.

results.title: Agro puppet
results.brief_description:
Agro was loud, messy and rude in the way that Australians loved. Performed by Jamie Dunn, the mischievous hand puppet became one of Australian children’s television’s most recognisable characters. He appeared on Boris’ Breakfast Club (1981–89), Wombat (1982–90), The Super Saturday Show (1989) and later fronted Agro’s Cartoon Connection (1990–97).

Agro’s appeal came from the gap between puppet and person. He behaved like a cheeky human host, but his ping-pong ball eyes, gravelly voice and shaggy fur made him clearly not human. Dunn usually stayed hidden behind furniture, while Agro joked with presenters, teased guests and often referred to being a puppet, including his unmoving limbs and the hand up his back. That gave Agro his ability to misbehave – the more obviously a puppet he was, the further the joke could go.

Since Dunn’s passing in 2026, Agro also carries the memory of a performer whose voice, timing and mischief made him so beloved.

results.title: Adventure Island
results.brief_description:
Adventure Island was a hugely popular ABC children’s television series, produced in Melbourne and screened five afternoons a week from 1967 to 1972. Created by Godfrey Philipp and John-Michael Howson, it grew out of The Magic Circle Club and followed stories set “far across the sea” in the Kingdom of Diddley-Dum-Diddley.

Puppets helped connect the fantasy world to the studio. Characters including Maxie Mouse, Samson the Cat, Crispian Cockatoo and Gracie Galah chatted with the host between story chapters, often sharing viewer drawings, riddles and jokes.

Built by Axel Axelrad, the puppets used different forms of operation. Samson was a large hand puppet, while the others were mechanical creations with rods inside or underneath the body to open the mouth or beak.

results.title: Sting
results.credit_line: Puppet created by Wētā Workshop Ltd, for Pictures in Paradise.
results.material_description: Nylon print plastic spider puppet, cables, wires, metal
results.brief_description:
In Sting (2024), a mysterious spider arrives from outer space, but its design comes from much closer to home: the Australian redback. Director Kiah Roache-Turner, who has severe arachnophobia, chose the redback because it’s the spider that frightens him most.

Sting grows throughout the film, shifting from a tiny skittering insect into a much larger threat. For Wētā Workshop, that meant designing a creature that could feel believable at different scales. Creative Director Richard Taylor described the challenge as bringing together “eight legs, all of them internally articulated”, along with the face, pedipalps, reflective eyes, pumping venom, dripping teeth and moving abdomen.

The largest version of Sting was an animatronic puppet built from 3D-printed parts, making it light, strong and flexible. Three puppeteers worked in close synchronisation to send its spindly legs creeping, gripping and scrambling through the narrow ventilation spaces where it lives and hunts.
